strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: agent count can affect exploration and coordination in opposing ways, making a fixed few-to-many curriculum inappropriate. Adapting self-paced learning to this setting is a practical contribution.

The experiments provide meaningful evidence of effectiveness. SPMARL improves over SPRLM on Simple-Spread and several Protoss tasks, while the appendix extends evaluation to Terran, Zerg, and two dense-reward BenchMARL tasks.

The presentation includes curriculum trajectories alongside target-task performance, five-seed results with confidence intervals, statistical comparisons, and a performance-threshold ablation. Algorithm descriptions, hyperparameter tables, and a source-code link help reproduction.
weaknesses: The central interpretation of critic loss as policy learning progress is insufficiently justified. Equation 4 measures prediction error, which can reflect critic underfitting or irreducible return variability. An accurately converged value function can coexist with a nonzero policy gradient, contrary to the motivation in Section 2. No direct measurements establish that this score predicts subsequent policy improvement. The results support a useful prioritization heuristic more clearly than the claimed mechanism.

The variance analysis does not establish lower estimation uncertainty. Appendix A.3.4 computes standard deviations across sampled contexts, mixing genuine differences between tasks with estimation noise. It also compares unnormalized episode returns against squared prediction errors, quantities with different scales and reward-scaling behavior, under separately evolving policies and curricula. Figures 7 and 10 therefore cannot substantiate the claimed variance advantage without matched-policy, fixed-context measurements and an appropriate normalization or signal-to-noise analysis.

The evaluation does not sufficiently isolate the claimed improvement in credit assignment. ALPGMM and VACL lack the same enforced progression toward the target distribution, so their weaker target performance can also reflect training-distribution mismatch. SPRLM is a useful matched baseline, but comparisons against smoothed or critic-estimated return scores within the same framework would help separate estimation effects from learning-progress selection. Direct evidence connecting the selected curricula to improved credit assignment is absent.

The baseline and prior-work coverage leave the contribution incompletely positioned. Simple-Spread uses a few-to-many Linear baseline even though the paper explains why that direction is unsuitable; a tuned many-to-few schedule would be more informative. Representing methods such as EPC through a generic linear schedule also omits their other mechanisms. Moreover, Prioritized Level Replay (Jiang et al., 2021) already studies value-error-based task prioritization and deserves explicit comparison when claiming novelty for this objective.

Claims of consistent superiority exceed the statistical evidence. Table 2 does not establish an advantage over SPRLM on XOR or ALPGMM on Protoss 5v5 and 6v6, and the dense-reward tasks show comparable performance. These results support a narrower claim of improvements on particular sparse-reward settings.

The curriculum score needs a more precise implementation specification. Equation 4 defines its target as the discounted return, whereas Appendix A.3.4 describes a one-step bootstrapped target; MAPPO also introduces GAE. These choices produce different task rankings. The manuscript should specify the actual target, normalization, aggregation, and timing relative to critic updates, and report curriculum-baseline hyperparameters sufficiently to assess tuning fairness.
